newsitem.title: USA: Groups to meet Jan 27 with U.S. on yield burning.
newsitem.headline: Groups to meet Jan 27 with U.S. on yield burning.

text.p: Municipal bond groups are set to meet with a top U.S. Treasury Department official on January 27 to outline their growing concerns with the IRS' controversial "yield burning" strategy, a representative of one of the groups said on Thursday.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond refinancing deals.

A 1996 Internal Revenue Service "closing agreement" plan says issuers can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by paying the Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest.

Bond lawyers and issuers urged the IRS at a three-hour hearing on Wednesday to scrap the plan and adopt a new one that puts the onus on Wall Street firms that knowingly sold inflated Treasuries to municipalities and on the few localities, if any, that were aware of the scam.

Frank Shafroth, director of policy and federal relations for the National League of Cities, said Thursday that municipal issuers' groups are scheduled to meet on the January 27 with Donald Lubick, Treasury's assistant secretary for tax policy.
Lubick is Treasury's point person on yield burning ever since Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin recused himself on the issue last year because of a possible conflict of interest.
IRS officials signaled at Wednesday's hearing that they may be willing to reconsider last year's closing agreement plan.

For instance, Michael Bailey, a senior IRS attorney specializing in tax-exempt bonds, asked witnesses whether they think the IRS and state and local governments could "work cooperatively" on a solution to the complex yield burning problem.

Groups likely to attend the upcoming Treasury summit are the Government Finance Officers Association, National Association of Bond Lawyers, National Conference of State Legislatures, and others, Shafroth said.
An IRS spokesperson was unavailable for comment.
